extracted.intended_audience: researchers, academics, and science policy readers (life-science community and general scientific public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and norms about how researchers, institutions, and funders should evaluate research and choose publication venues — emphasizing scientific quality, incentives, editorial practice, and open access. The piece argues for resisting prestige-driven incentives and for favoring openness and substantive merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate science by intrinsic quality, not journal brand
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is the quality of the science, not the journal's brand, that matters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schekman advocates that researchers, funders, universities, and hiring/tenure/grant committees should judge papers on their scientific merit rather than the prestige of the journal in which they appear. The author calls on funders and universities to tell committees not to judge papers by where they are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incentives that reward flashiness over importance
rubrics_metrics.description: “The prevailing structures of personal reputation and career advancement mean the biggest rewards often follow the flashiest work, not the best.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should prioritize research importance and rigor over novelty-for-splash; systems of reward should be reformed so that career advancement and reputation are not tied primarily to 'flashy' results. The piece likens this to breaking the bonus-culture that drives harmful incentives in other fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let publication pressure drive questionable practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure to publish in “luxury” journals encouraged researchers to cut corners and pursue trendy fields of science instead of doing more important work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to perverse incentives: if evaluation criteria emphasize venue prestige, researchers may engage in risky shortcuts or chase fashions. Committees and evaluators should design assessment criteria that reduce pressure to prioritize venue over methodological rigor and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer editorial leadership by active scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: Schekman criticizes editors who were not active scientists but professionals who favored studies that were likely to make a splash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal editorial decisions should be informed by experienced active researchers rather than only professional editors whose selection priorities may favor sensational results. Evaluators and authors should favor venues with editorial practices that emphasize scientific judgment by peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor open-access publishing and permissive licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: eLife content is available for free and is under a Creative Commons Attribution License (CC-BY). Schekman advocates open-access journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing where to publish or which work to rely on, prefer journals that provide free public access and use permissive licenses (e.g., CC-BY) to align with broader access and transparency goals. Funders and institutions should support and incentivize open-access outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective action (boycott) as a corrective for perverse publishing incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Schekman's lab would no longer send research papers to leading scientific journals like Nature, Cell and Science; he calls scientists to take action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One recommended corrective is for researchers and labs to withhold submissions from high-prestige journals that, in the author's view, perpetuate harmful incentives. Institutions and funders can support such actions by changing evaluation rules so venue prestige is not rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform institutional evaluation procedures to de-emphasize venue
rubrics_metrics.description: He called scientists to take action and funders and universities to tell the committees that decide on grants and positions not to judge papers by where they are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical institutional steps include explicit policy guidance to hiring, promotion, and grant committees to evaluate the content and quality of work directly rather than using journal name as a proxy; implement assessment processes that examine methods, data, and substantive contributions.
